title: Purpose and result: ἵνα, ὅπως, ὥστε

objectives.can: Recognise a purpose clause with ἵνα or ὅπως and distinguish it from ἵνα giving content or result.

explanation.summary: ἵνα and ὅπως with the subjunctive usually give the purpose of an action: 'in order that'. But ἵνα also introduces what someone asks, commands or wants, where it is not a purpose at all; and ὥστε with the infinitive states a result. The same little word can do different jobs, and the verb it follows decides which.

sections.heading: Purpose: ἵνα or ὅπως with the subjunctive
body: A purpose clause tells why the main action is done. In Greek it is introduced by ἵνα or by ὅπως, and its verb is in the subjunctive. John 20:31 says why the book was written: ταῦτα δὲ γέγραπται ἵνα πιστεύητε. The subjunctive after ἵνα is not a sign of doubt. The clause names the aim, not whether it will be met.

The negative is ἵνα μή or ὅπως μή: 'so that not', 'lest'. In Mark 3:9 Jesus tells the disciples to have a small boat ready ἵνα μὴ θλίβωσιν αὐτόν, 'so that they might not crush him'. In Matthew 6:18 the aim of fasting in secret is put with ὅπως μὴ φανῇς.

Present and aorist subjunctives differ here as in the last lesson, by aspect, not by time. After ἵνα the verb is often an aorist, but the present is common when the action is continuing or repeated: ἵνα πιστεύητε in John 20:31 is a present subjunctive in this edition, though some manuscripts have an aorist there. Do not build a theory on the tense alone.

ὅπως is the less common of the two in the New Testament. It can also mean 'how', and when it introduces a purpose it is much like ἵνα. The Sermon on the Mount, in Matthew 5:16 and 6:2, uses it for the aim of an action.

sections.heading: Not every ἵνα gives a purpose: content
body: After verbs of asking, urging, commanding, wanting and the like, ἵνα with the subjunctive says what is asked, urged or wanted. This is called a content clause (grammarians also say noun clause or complement clause). The clause answers the question 'what?' and not 'why?'. In Mark 5:18 the man παρεκάλει ἵνα μετ' αὐτοῦ ᾖ: he begged that he might be with Jesus. The clause gives the content of his request. An English infinitive often does the same work: 'asked him to…'.

ἵνα also follows a noun or a pronoun that needs to be explained, such as ἐντολή, 'commandment': in John 13:34 the new commandment is ἵνα ἀγαπᾶτε ἀλλήλους, 'that you love one another'. In John 17:3 the same pattern says what eternal life is: αὕτη δέ ἐστιν ἡ αἰώνιος ζωὴ ἵνα γινώσκωσι… A clause that spells out what a noun means in this way is called explanatory or epexegetic.

A quick test: if you can ask 'in order to do what?' or 'why?', it is a purpose clause. If you can ask 'what is requested, ordered or meant?', it is a content clause. A third possibility is a clause with ὥστε, taken next.

Typical neighbour

sections.heading: Result: ὥστε with the infinitive
body: ὥστε usually states a result: something that followed, so that it is true now. With the infinitive, as in Matthew 8:24, it states the result as a consequence: σεισμὸς μέγας ἐγένετο ἐν τῇ θαλάσσῃ, ὥστε τὸ πλοῖον καλύπτεσθαι. The result is what happened as a consequence, 'so that the boat was being covered by the waves'. A purpose clause states what the doer aims at; a result clause states what comes about, and it may or may not have been intended.

When ὥστε takes the infinitive, the subject of the infinitive is in the accusative (τὸ πλοῖον) and the verb is not a finite verb. With the indicative, as in John 3:16 and Matthew 12:12, ὥστε states the result as an actual fact, and the clause can read like an inference: 'so that', 'so then'. ὥστε can also stand at the start of a new sentence with the sense 'so then, therefore'.
The forms of the infinitive are taught in lesson G4.2.1. For now it is enough to notice that an infinitive after ὥστε is a sign of result, not of purpose.

sections.heading: Putting it together
body: Look at the conjunction first and the verb second. ἵνα or ὅπως with a subjunctive: purpose, content or explanation. ὥστε with an infinitive or an indicative: result. Then decide among the first three by looking at the verb before the conjunction: an action done for a reason points to purpose; a verb of asking, ordering or wanting, or a noun that needs explaining, points to content or explanation.

misunderstandings: Taking every ἵνα as 'in order that'. After verbs of asking and wanting, and after nouns like ἐντολή, it only says what the request or the commandment is: 'that'.
Reading ὥστε with the infinitive as a statement of aim. It states what happened as a result, whether or not anyone intended it.
Thinking the subjunctive after ἵνα means 'might' in every case. The mood marks the clause as aim or content, not as uncertainty.
Treating ὅπως as always meaning 'how'. In the New Testament it often introduces a purpose, like ἵνα.

deeper.heading: Where purpose and result meet
body: The lines between the clauses are not always sharp, and the New Testament has places where grammarians disagree. In John 9:2, the question about who sinned ἵνα τυφλὸς γεννηθῇ has been taken as a purpose ('in order that he be born blind') and as a result ('so that he was born blind'). Both views are held, and the grammar by itself does not settle it. Read each case in its context and say plainly when the form leaves it open.

deeper.heading: Content clauses and the infinitive
body: Classical Greek used an infinitive after verbs of asking and commanding where the New Testament more often uses ἵνα. The Greek of the New Testament still has infinitives with such verbs, so both patterns occur side by side. The wider use of ἵνα is one of the visible differences between the Greek of the New Testament and classical prose.

examples.analysis: ἵνα πιστεύητε: the purpose of the book. πιστεύητε is a present active subjunctive, second person plural. The second ἵνα clause, ἵνα πιστεύοντες ζωὴν ἔχητε, adds a further purpose; the verb is ἔχητε, present subjunctive, and the participle πιστεύοντες describes how the result is reached.

examples.analysis: ὅπως ἴδωσιν … καὶ δοξάσωσιν: a purpose clause with ὅπως and two aorist active subjunctives, third person plural. It follows the imperative λαμψάτω and gives the aim of the shining: that people see the good works and praise the Father.

examples.analysis: παρεκάλει: the man begged. ἵνα μετ' αὐτοῦ ᾖ is not a purpose but the content of the request, 'that he might be with him'. ᾖ is a present subjunctive of εἰμί, third person singular. The neighbour of ἵνα is a verb of asking.

examples.analysis: The new commandment is spelt out by ἵνα ἀγαπᾶτε ἀλλήλους: the clause is explanatory, saying what the commandment is. The second ἵνα clause, with ἀγαπᾶτε again, repeats the commandment and adds its model: you too, as I loved you. Both verbs are present active subjunctives, second person plural; the shape of the verb, ἀγαπᾶτε, is the same as the indicative, so the ἵνα is what shows the mood.

practice.prompt: What does ἵνα μὴ θλίβωσιν αὐτόν (words 12–15) express?

options: A negative purpose: so that they might not crush him
A result: so that they did not crush him
The content of an order: that they should crush him
An emphatic denial about the future
practice.explain: ἵνα μή with the subjunctive is the negative purpose clause. It gives the reason for having the boat ready. Result would be introduced by ὥστε, and οὐ μή would be needed for an emphatic denial.

practice.prompt: ἵνα οἱ λίθοι οὗτοι ἄρτοι γένωνται (words 12–17) follows the command εἰπέ. What is the clause?

options: A condition
A content clause: what he is told to say
A result clause
A purpose clause giving the reason for Jesus' answer
practice.explain: The tempter is telling Jesus what to say: the ἵνα clause gives the content of the order, 'say that these stones become bread'. It does not give a reason for an action already named.

practice.prompt: δεήθητε is a command: 'ask the Lord of the harvest'. What does the ὅπως clause (words 6–8) give?

options: A condition: if he sends out workers
The content of the request: what they are to ask for
A result that has already happened
A question introduced by ὅπως, 'how'
practice.explain: After a verb of asking, ὅπως with the subjunctive ἐκβάλῃ says what is asked, as ἵνα does in Mark 5:18. It answers 'what?' rather than 'why?'.

practice.prompt: In this verse ὥστε is followed by the infinitive βυθίζεσθαι (word 20). What does the clause tell the reader?

options: That they asked someone to sink the boats
That the boats were filling so much that they began to sink: a result
That the boats sank as a punishment
That they filled the boats in order that they would sink
practice.explain: ὥστε with the infinitive βυθίζεσθαι is a result clause: it says what followed from the full catch. Nobody aimed at sinking the boats, so purpose is out.

check.prompt: In this verse there are two clauses, one with ὥστε and one with ἵνα. How do they differ?

options: ὥστε with the indicative states the actual result of God's love; ἵνα with the subjunctive gives the purpose of the gift
Both are result clauses
Both are content clauses
ἵνα states the actual result and ὥστε the purpose
check.explain: ἔδωκεν is an indicative after ὥστε: the giving is stated as a fact that resulted from the love. The subjunctives ἀπόληται and ἔχῃ after ἵνα state what the giving is for. The first clause states what happened; the second states what the happening was meant to bring about.

check.prompt: How is ὅπως μὴ φανῇς (words 0–2) best understood?

options: 'How you do not appear': an indirect question
'So that you did not appear': a result clause
'That you should not appear': the content of a request
'So that you do not appear': a negative purpose clause
check.explain: ὅπως with the subjunctive φανῇς and the negative μή is a negative purpose: the reason for the secrecy of the fast. It is not an indirect question, though ὅπως can mean 'how' elsewhere.

check.prompt: What does ἵνα γινώσκωσι (words 6–7) do in the sentence 'this is eternal life …'?

options: It is a hortatory subjunctive
It states a result of eternal life
It gives the purpose of the verb ἐστιν
It explains αὕτη, saying what eternal life is
check.explain: The pronoun αὕτη needs to be filled out. The ἵνα clause names what it refers to: that they know. It is explanatory, and the verb ἐστιν is a linking verb, so there is no action whose purpose could be stated.

check.prompt: ἵνα … ποιήσῃς ἡμῖν (words 13–19) follows θέλομεν. What is the clause?

quoted.title: Mark
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: A purpose clause: they come in order that Jesus may do something
A result clause
An indefinite relative clause
A content clause: what they want
check.explain: θέλομεν is a verb of wanting; the ἵνα clause says what is wanted. The relative clause ὃ ἐὰν αἰτήσωμέν σε is inside it: 'whatever we ask you'. It is the ἵνα that gives the content.

check.prompt: ὥστε … καθῆσθαι (words 6–11): what is ὥστε doing here?

options: Introducing the content of a request
Introducing a result: so that he got into a boat and sat
Introducing a wish
Introducing an aim: in order that he sit in the boat
check.explain: The crowds gathered in such numbers that Jesus got into the boat and sat down. The infinitive καθῆσθαι with ὥστε states a consequence; the accusative αὐτόν is the subject of the infinitive, with the participle ἐμβάντα.

check.prompt: What does ὅπως μὴ καυχήσηται πᾶσα σάρξ express?

options: A request: that no one boast
A purpose: so that no one may boast
A result that has already happened
A wish: may no one boast
check.explain: ὅπως μή with the aorist subjunctive καυχήσηται gives the aim, stated negatively. The clause does not depend on a verb of asking, so it is not content.

check.prompt: What does the ὅπως clause add after the command to pray?

options: The aim of the prayer and the confession: so that you may be healed
The content of the prayer only
A consequence which has already happened
A question: how will you be healed?
check.explain: ἰαθῆτε is an aorist passive subjunctive, second person plural, after ὅπως. The clause names the intended outcome of the confession and prayer in the two imperatives before it.

check.prompt: ὥστε begins this clause, but the verb that follows it is ἔξεστιν, an indicative. How is it best read?

quoted.title: Matthew
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. options: As a conclusion drawn from what has been said: 'so it is lawful'
As a purpose clause, with the infinitive ποιεῖν
As a content clause after a verb of asking
As a wish
check.explain: ὥστε with an indicative states the result as a fact, and here it reads as an inference from the comparison of a man with a sheep. The infinitive ποιεῖν depends on ἔξεστιν, not on ὥστε.

reading.why: The saying about the light of the world ends in a ὅπως purpose clause (5:16). The verses that follow return to the subjunctive of the last lesson: μή with the aorist subjunctive in 5:17, οὐ μή in 5:18 and 5:20, and ἕως ἄν, ὃς ἐάν and ἐὰν μή. Reading them side by side shows how each construction looks in a real text.
